meta.titre: Geographical Fieldwork Techniques: instruments, measurements and their limitations
meta.sous_theme: Techniques for rivers, towns, slopes, soils and weather

sections.contenu_markdown: A group of Upper Sixth students stands in a small stream with a tape measure, a stopwatch and an orange. One holds the tape across the channel, one drops the orange upstream and calls the time when it passes the downstream mark, one writes in the notebook. Later the same group asks shoppers in a market to fill in a questionnaire and counts pedestrians at a junction. Paper 3 expects you to describe such techniques exactly: what was measured, with what, how often, how accurately and with what weakness. This course gives you the standard techniques and the habit of judging them.

items: Velocity is distance divided by time.
The area of a trapezium is half the sum of its parallel sides multiplied by the distance between them.
A questionnaire is a set of written questions answered by a sample of people.
A river channel has a bed, banks and a cross-section, which is the shape of the channel seen at right angles to the flow.

sections.titre: Fieldwork techniques and how to describe them
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Choosing and describing a technique
For every technique state **what** it measures, the **equipment**, **where and how often** it is used and **one limitation**. Good fieldwork repeats readings, follows a sampling plan and records results on a prepared sheet.

| Technique | What it measures | Equipment | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Channel width and depth | cross-section of a river | tape measure, metre rule | depth varies between readings; soft beds and banks |
| Float method | surface velocity | float (an orange or cork), stopwatch, measured stretch | wind and obstacles affect the float |
| Clinometer survey | slope angle | clinometer, ranging poles, tape | sighting errors; one profile may not be typical |
| Bed-load sampling | size and shape of pebbles | ruler or calipers | choosing larger pebbles by eye gives bias |
| Soil sampling | depth, texture, moisture, acidity | auger, trowel, pH kit | small sample; kits are not precise |
| Weather recording | temperature, rainfall, wind | thermometer, rain gauge, anemometer | only a short period is recorded |
| Questionnaire or interview | opinions and behaviour | printed sheet | bias, refusals, leading questions |
| Counts of people or vehicles | flow at a point | tally sheet, stopwatch | one day may not be typical |
| Land-use mapping | pattern of land use | base map, colour key | classification is subjective |
| Environmental quality survey | quality of surroundings | scoring sheet | scores differ between observers |

### Accuracy and reliability
Accuracy improves when you repeat measurements and take the mean, use the equipment in the same way each time and let a second person check the readings. Choose sites by a sampling method and record the date, time and weather, because these affect rivers, soils and counts.

### Safety and ethics
Work in groups, avoid deep or fast water, ask permission before entering private land or questioning people, and do not record personal names unless they are needed.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks you to measure or calculate the flow of a stream or to compare sites along it.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Measure the width, then the depth at equal intervals across the channel. The cross-sectional area is the sum of the strips, each equal to the mean of two neighbouring depths multiplied by the interval. Time a float over a marked stretch several times, take the mean time and calculate the surface velocity. Surface water flows faster than the average because the bed and banks slow the rest, so a correction factor is applied to the velocity; the factor depends on the bed and is usually between 0.8 and 0.9, so use the value given in the question. Discharge is

$$
Q = A \times v
$$

where $Q$ is the discharge in $\text{m}^3\,\text{s}^{-1}$, $A$ the cross-sectional area in $\text{m}^2$ and $v$ the mean velocity in $\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. After heavy rain both $A$ and $v$ increase, so discharge rises.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question concerns shopping, traffic, land use or quality of the environment in a town or village.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A good questionnaire uses mostly **closed** questions (tick a box) for easy counting and a few **open** questions for reasons. Avoid leading questions such as one that suggests the answer, test the sheet on a few people first (a pilot) and explain the purpose politely. Counts of pedestrians or vehicles must be taken at the same time on the same days, with a tally sheet and a fixed period. In land-use mapping each building or plot is coloured on a base map according to a key. In an environmental quality survey each site is scored on several criteria (litter, noise, building condition) on a scale such as -2 to +2, and the totals are compared; the weakness is that scores are subjective.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks how to measure relief, soil properties or weather at a site.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Slope: mark points along a line, place a ranging pole at the end of each section, read the angle with a clinometer at the same height on the pole, and measure the distance with a tape. The gradient can be expressed as an angle or as 1 in $n$, where $n = \frac{1}{\tan \theta}$. Soil: take samples at fixed intervals with an auger, record depth, colour, texture by feel and the pH of a mixture with water. Weather: place the thermometer in shade, the rain gauge in an open place clear of trees and read all instruments at the same time each day.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A student team surveyed a small stream. The channel was 6.0 m wide, and depths were measured every 1.0 m across it, starting at one bank: 0, 0.30, 0.50, 0.60, 0.40, 0.20 and 0 m. An orange was timed over a 10 m stretch three times: 9, 10 and 11 seconds. The team used a correction factor of 0.8.

(a) Calculate the cross-sectional area.
(b) Calculate the corrected mean velocity.
(c) Calculate the discharge.
(d) Give one reason why the result may be inaccurate.

etapes.action: Find the area of each 1.0 m strip.
etapes.justification: Each strip is a trapezium, with area equal to the mean of two neighbouring depths multiplied by 1.0 m.
The cross-sectional area is the total of all strips.

etapes.action: Calculate the mean time and the surface velocity.
etapes.justification: The mean of repeated timings reduces random error; velocity is distance divided by time.
Surface water moves faster than the average of the whole cross-section.
Discharge is the volume passing a point each second, area multiplied by mean velocity.
A full answer always judges the reliability of the method.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Depth was measured at only seven points, so the shape of the bed between them is estimated; the float may have been moved by wind or caught by stones; the correction factor is an average value.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The cross-sectional area is **2.00 m²**, the corrected mean velocity is **0.8 m/s** and the discharge is **1.6 m³/s**. The result is only an estimate: readings were few, the float is affected by wind and obstacles, and a single day does not show the usual flow. Repeating the readings, measuring depth at closer intervals and measuring on several days would improve reliability.

items.erreur_markdown: Timing the float only once, close to the bank, and using that value as the velocity of the whole stream.
items.pourquoi_faux: Water moves slowest near the banks and bed because of friction, and a single reading cannot show random error.
items.correction_markdown: Release the float at several points across the channel, repeat each run at least three times and use the mean time, then apply the correction factor to turn surface velocity into mean velocity.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving the discharge as $1.6\ \text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$, or confusing velocity with discharge.
items.pourquoi_faux: Velocity is a speed in metres per second; discharge is a volume per second, so its unit is cubic metres per second.

items.erreur_markdown: Using the surface velocity directly in the discharge calculation without a correction factor, or applying a factor without saying why.
items.pourquoi_faux: The surface of a stream flows faster than the average, so discharge would be overestimated. A factor used without explanation gains little credit.
items.correction_markdown: State that friction with the bed and banks slows the water below the surface, apply the factor given (or a stated one such as 0.8), and show the corrected velocity.

items.erreur_markdown: "I used a clinometer to measure the slope." (and nothing more)
items.pourquoi_faux: The answer names the instrument but gives no method: where, how many points, how the angle was read and what the weakness was.
items.correction_markdown: Describe the points chosen, the ranging poles and the tape, the angle read at the same height on each pole, and a limitation such as sighting error.

items.erreur_markdown: A questionnaire question such as "Do you agree that the market is too dirty?"
items.pourquoi_faux: It is a leading question: it pushes the respondent towards one answer and biases the data.
items.correction_markdown: Use a neutral wording, for example "How would you rate the cleanliness of the market?" with choices from very poor to very good, and pilot the question.

items.enonce_markdown:
A student timed a float over a 20 m stretch of stream three times: 15 s, 16 s and 17 s.

(a) Calculate the mean time.
(b) Calculate the surface velocity.
(c) Calculate the corrected velocity using a factor of 0.8.
(d) Explain why the surface velocity is greater than the mean velocity of the whole stream.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Mean time $= \frac{15 + 16 + 17}{3} = $ **16 s**.

(b) $v = \frac{20\ \text{m}}{16\ \text{s}} = $ **1.25 m/s**.

(c) $1.25 \times 0.8 = $ **1.0 m/s**.

(d) Friction with the bed and banks slows the water there, while the surface layer in the middle of the channel meets the least resistance, so a float on the surface travels faster than the average.

items.enonce_markdown:
A stream is 4 m wide. Depths measured every 1 m from one bank are 0, 0.20, 0.50, 0.30 and 0 m. A float travels 10 m in 16 s and the correction factor is 0.8.

(a) Calculate the cross-sectional area.
(b) Calculate the corrected velocity.
(c) Calculate the discharge.
(d) State how discharge would change after heavy rain and explain why.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Strips: $\frac{0 + 0.20}{2} = 0.10$; $\frac{0.20 + 0.50}{2} = 0.35$; $\frac{0.50 + 0.30}{2} = 0.40$; $\frac{0.30 + 0}{2} = 0.15$. Area $= 0.10 + 0.35 + 0.40 + 0.15 = $ **1.0 m²**.

(b) Surface velocity $= \frac{10}{16} = 0.625\ \text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$; corrected velocity $= 0.625 \times 0.8 = $ **0.5 m/s**.

(c) $Q = 1.0 \times 0.5 = $ **0.5 m³/s**.

(d) Discharge increases. More water enters the channel from run-off, so the depth and the cross-sectional area increase, and the velocity also increases because the deeper channel loses less energy to friction with the bed and banks.

items.enonce_markdown:
A class tested the hypothesis that pebbles become smaller downstream. At each of two sites they measured the longest axis (in mm) of 10 pebbles.

- Site 1 (upstream): 92, 85, 78, 88, 95, 70, 82, 90, 76, 84
- Site 2 (downstream): 41, 38, 52, 45, 36, 48, 40, 44, 50, 46

(a) Describe a suitable way of choosing the pebbles at each site.
(b) Calculate the mean size at each site and the percentage decrease from Site 1 to Site 2.
(c) Explain two reasons for the pattern and suggest one limitation of the survey.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) At each site walk along a line across the channel, stop at regular intervals (or use random numbers), close the eyes or look away, pick up the pebble touched by the finger at the toe, and measure its longest axis with a ruler. This avoids choosing pebbles that look interesting or large.

(b) Site 1: sum $= 840$, mean $= \frac{840}{10} = $ **84 mm**. Site 2: sum $= 440$, mean $= \frac{440}{10} = $ **44 mm**. Decrease $= \frac{84 - 44}{84} \times 100 = $ **47.6%**.

(c) Reasons: pebbles knock against each other and the bed (attrition) and are worn down by the load carried by the river (abrasion), so they become smaller and rounder; the river also loses energy and carries only smaller material further downstream while larger stones are left behind. Limitation: only two sites and ten pebbles at each, so the sample is small and does not show whether the decrease is regular; a tributary or local rock outcrop could also change the size.

items_markdown: Describe each technique with what it measures, equipment, where and how often, and a limitation.

Discharge $Q = A \times v$ in cubic metres per second; the area is found by adding the strips between depth readings, and the float velocity is corrected because the surface flows faster than the average.
Repeat readings and use the mean; record date, time and weather; follow a sampling plan to avoid bias.
A questionnaire uses mostly closed questions, neutral wording and a pilot; counts must be taken at the same times.
Environmental quality scores, land-use classes and clinometer readings are subjective or imprecise: say so in the evaluation.
Safety and respect for people and property are part of good fieldwork.
